title: Permute-then-Adapt: Weak-to-Strong Contrastive Image-Text Adaptation
claim: A fixed similarity threshold works on one dataset but admits many false positives when the null distribution shifts; adaptive calibration controls error.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, shared axes, vertical threshold lines over histograms, annotation boxes
description: Two side-by-side histogram panels with Cosine Similarity (0 to 0.4) on the x-axis and Density on the y-axis. The left panel shows a narrow light-blue null distribution centered near 0.15. A red dashed vertical line marks the fixed threshold at 0.3 and a green solid line marks PTA at 0.26. A black-bordered box reads 'Noise Accepted: 0.2%'. The right panel shows a wider, right-shifted orange null distribution centered near 0.18. The red fixed line at 0.3 now cuts into the tail, and the accepted-noise region is shaded red. The green PTA line sits further right at 0.32. A red-bordered box reads 'Noise Accepted: 2.4% (12x Higher Error)'. Legends sit above each panel. The eye goes first to the contrasting vertical lines and the red callout on the right.
caption: The risk of uncalibrated heuristics. While a fixed threshold (red dashed) works on COCO (Left), it fails on fine-grained Stanford Cars (Right), where the random-pairing null distribution shifts rightward. The fixed threshold accepts 12$\times$ more false positives from the null on Cars. In contrast, PTA (green solid) estimates a dataset-specific permutation null and adapts its cutoff to control Type-I error relative to that reference at level $\alpha$, up to calibration approximation error.
abstract: Image-text alignment models such as CLIP are typically trained with contrastive learning, where unpaired examples are treated as strict negatives. While this assumption introduces noise by penalising semantically related pairs, existing solutions often rely on heuristic similarity thresholds that lack statistical grounding and sensitivity to dataset-specific noise distributions. In this paper, we propose Permute-then-Adapt (PTA), a framework that leverages efficient weak models to identify missed positives while controlling Type-I error relative to a conditional permutation reference, up to calibration approximation error. Unlike standard distillation or arbitrary thresholding, PTA estimates a random-pairing reference distribution from the weak teacher's similarity scores and uses its upper tail, determined by $Î±$, to select auxiliary positives. The calibrated positive set is then trained against by a single multi-positive contrastive objective: each anchor maximises the total probability mass it assigns to its positive set. Offline calibration with the weak model adds negligible training overhead. Experiments show gains over heuristic soft-label approaches in object recognition, cross-modal retrieval, and data efficiency. Project repository: https://github.com/JinhaoLee/Permute-then-Adapt.
